collections.title: Rainy-day rescue
collections.when_to_use: Recess just got cancelled and 25 kids are stuck inside. Pick any three. They run back-to-back with no setup between them.

picks.curator_note: Ten minutes of full-body movement. The fastest way to burn off rain-stuck wiggles.
Competitive but silent: the only indoor game that calms the room while it plays.
Zero materials, huge laughs. Works while you quietly re-arrange the room.
Everyone participates; nobody needs any skill, supplies, or setup.
Scales from silly to clever. Pairs perfectly with a restless afternoon.
Reads like pure mischief, practices language. They'll never notice the learning.
Steady hands after chaos: a calm-down disguised as a building challenge.
A full story in twenty minutes with nothing but imagination and dice.
Rediscovers your own classroom, pair up kids who never talk.
The old reliable: when energy peaks, chair count beats any fancy game.
Big rallies, zero breakage risk, hallway-safe and endlessly replayable.
Matching plus fine motor: quietly absorbs twenty minutes of indoor time.

collections.title: First day of the program
collections.when_to_use: New faces, new room, first impressions. Run these in order on day one. Names first, kindness last.

picks.curator_note: Names stick fast when every kid says them out loud twice in one game.
The day-two sequel. Run it and watch last week's strangers light up.
Gets every kid talking to five kids they don't know yet.
Same magic, written down, a lifeline for the shy joiners.
Names with a beat, the wigglers remember this one all year.
Silent sorting means nobody needs words to belong on day one.
Sets the tone immediately: this room is a kind place.
Passes warmth around the circle, literally hand to hand.
The classic first-day reveal. Strangers become interesting fast.
Finds the surprising thing three kids all share.
One word each: by the end, the whole room owns the same story.
Ends the first day on a giggle for the younger half of the group.

collections.title: Last 10 minutes
collections.when_to_use: The clock is dying and dismissal is ten minutes of chaos. These run cold. No setup, and every one ends with a settled room.

picks.curator_note: Five shapes, five breaths. The reset button you can run daily.
Ten near-silent minutes that feel like magic to a loud room.
Belly breathing with a stuffed buddy riding on top. Little ones leave settled.
Counts down to dismissal with movement instead of fidgeting.
One fast round while coats go on. Names and laughter to close the day.
Silly movement that eats ten minutes and leaves everyone smiling.
One song, freeze on cue, energy out, coats on, done.
Ten minutes, one voice, total focus: the classic closer.
Zero setup. Just one question the whole group can argue about.
Fifteen minutes of kindness on the way out the door.

collections.title: Field-trip bus ride
collections.when_to_use: Thirty seats, one long road, no chaos allowed. Seated, quiet-ish, and everything fits on a tray table.

picks.curator_note: The perfect bus game, one voice at a time, whole bus listening.
Works beautifully down a bus aisle, seat row to seat row.
Debate fuel for mile forty, no materials required.
Pass-the-paper storytelling: the bus writes a novel by arrival.
Mad Libs at full volume, check with the driver first.
Quiet, absorbing coloring for the long middle stretch.
Print-and-go calm, pack a stack of copies before you board.
Tiny dice, endless plots, fits on a seatback tray.
Every window becomes a science lab; bring the sky along.
The bus provides the sound effects. The kids build the story.
Learn the one thing nobody knew about the kid in seat 12B.
Write one kind postcard before you arrive, hand them out at pickup.

collections.title: Sub Tub essentials
collections.when_to_use: The ten cards every sub folder needs. Pairs with the Sub Tub kit (sub.html). Every pick runs from its card alone: no hidden setup, no weird supplies.

picks.curator_note: Foolproof energy burner. The sub just presses play.
Every sub knows it, every kid obeys it, zero explanation needed.
No materials, no mess, nothing to follow up on.
Quiet competition, the room practically manages itself.
Reading practice that feels like mischief.
A full language block from a cup of dice.
Discussion for any age. Fills any gap in the day.
Quiet seat work a sub can stretch to forty-five minutes.
Guaranteed weird results. No drawing skill needed to run it.
Kindness-based: leaves the room better than the sub found it.
Paper only. The classic that has never once failed.
Spring-storm backup: the whole class becomes the weather, zero materials, ten loud minutes.

collections.title: Winter party night
collections.when_to_use: The winter pack's greatest hits. Pairs with the Party Planner's ❄️ Winter theme (party.html). Rotate these through three stations and close with the countdown.

picks.curator_note: Every kid leaves with a window-worthy snowflake, and it needs zero prep.
The take-home gift parents actually keep.
Build with paper shapes, no royal-icing disasters.
Snowball fight plus math facts: this is your movement station.
The dance break between stations, one playlist, done.
Practice the big countdown. Pure party energy to close the night.
Irresistible craft that doubles as a party favor.
A collaborative wreath for the classroom door.
The quiet reflection corner while glue dries.
Everyone contributes one square, hang it in January.
Hang them outside and catch the morning light.
One outrageous winter story, told by the whole party at once.

collections.title: No-prep lifesavers
collections.when_to_use: Grab-and-go, zero setup, any time the plan falls apart. If you only memorize one collection, make it this one.

picks.curator_note: The opener that has never missed. Run it with total strangers.
Any topic, any group, instantly running in under a minute.
One word each, the story surprises everyone, including you.
Five minutes to a measurably warmer room.
The team-builder that needs nothing but hands.
Silent sorting by birthdays, no words, no materials, full focus.
Kids will sneak kindness all week after this one.
Gratitude in ten minutes, send them home at pickup.
One story passed around the circle; everybody owns the ending.
The littles' favorite, zero setup, maximum joy.
Ten minutes, one voice, total focus.
Tag without touching, perfect for mixed ages outdoors.

collections.title: Calm-down corner
collections.when_to_use: For the wired, the wobbly, and the overstimulated. Keep these on a ring by the quiet corner. Any kid can self-select.

picks.curator_note: Five shapes, five breaths, the reset button.
Follow the bell until the sound disappears, instant quiet.
Belly breathing with a buddy riding on top.
Shake it, watch it settle. The metaphor does the teaching.
Name your tools before the big feelings arrive.
Repetitive and absorbing, minds quiet down on their own.
Simple patterns, no decisions, pure calm.
Three good things. The fastest perspective shift there is.
Gentle storytelling with zero pressure to perform.
The outdoor reset: five sounds, four textures, one calmer kid.
Stacking stones forces slow, careful focus.
Pin a leaf for something good. The corner grows its own forest.

collections.title: Spring burst
collections.when_to_use: The air is warm, the kids are wiggly, and everything is blooming. This is the spring 2027 pack's greatest hits plus the Vault's best older spring picks, crafts, puddle science, outdoor games, and spring-holiday stations.

picks.curator_note: Fifteen minutes, coffee filters, total magic. The fastest spring win in the pack.
Rocks from the yard become garden art; hide them for other classes to find.
The after-rain classic, kids who claim to hate science love worm duty.
Zero materials, pure joy. Rain boots required, dignity optional.
Engineering with plastic eggs. The design iteration is the lesson.
Toss-and-grow: the rare craft that keeps working after class ends.
The spring classic that was already in the Vault, now properly tagged.
Forced bulbs in jars: weeks of delicious 'is it blooming yet' anticipation.
Let the kids design the hunt. Hiding is more fun than finding.
Stuck inside by a spring storm? Become the storm.
The marble 'egg' test turns nest-building into a real engineering challenge.
One trash bag, one tally chart, one class that never sees litter the same way.

collections.title: Summer splash
collections.when_to_use: The days are long, the kids are restless, and the hose is already out. This is the summer 2027 pack's greatest hits plus the Vault's best older summer picks. Water play, camp games, sun crafts, beat-the-heat backups, and July 4th stations.

picks.curator_note: Step back after every catch. The rare game where staying dry is the skill.
Duck-duck-goose with a wet sponge: instant summer legend status.
Over heads, cup to cup, the loudest fifteen minutes of the week.
Chalk targets, wet splat marks, argued line calls like pros.
How low before you're soaked? The heat-wave answer.
The indoor rescue for scorcher days: salt, droppers, real melting science.
The camp classic, one knot, endless trading.
The sun does the printing; the kids just arrange and wait.
Simplified so it actually finishes inside 45 minutes.
Draw it, run it, then let the kids redesign it.
Red, white, and blue floats, parade the whole route.
Trace one shadow all solstice day; the sun draws the graph.

collections.title: Haunted halls
collections.when_to_use: October is here and the program needs its Halloween spine: the Halloween 2026 pack's greatest hits plus the Vault's best older not-too-spooky picks, crafts, costume games, mild-thrill science, harvest anchors, trick-or-treat alternatives, and the allergy-aware must-dos.

picks.curator_note: All the pumpkin fun, zero knives. The young-kid classic that starts every October.
Tissue ghosts on a string: the fastest room transformation in the Vault.
Cardstock monsters with real 3D horns and fangs, costume-station ready.
Every costume gets its strut and its narrator moment.
Freeze when the music stops, in your spookiest pose.
Peeled grapes, cold spaghetti: mild thrills, lights on, zero scares.
The jack-o'-lantern erupts, baking soda, vinegar, dish soap.
Candy dyes split into rainbows on coffee filters, real separation science.
The harvest anchor: blind taste-test, vote, graph the results.
The allergy-aware must-do: teal pumpkin, non-food treat box, every kid included.
The parking-lot alternative, planned by the kids themselves.
Deliver treats instead of collecting them, the kindness flip.

collections.title: Grateful gathering
collections.when_to_use: November is here and the program needs its Thanksgiving spine: the Thanksgiving 2026 pack's greatest hits plus the Vault's best older gratitude picks. Crafts, harvest games, Thanksgiving STEM, gratitude practices, friendsgiving plans, and giving-back projects. Inclusive by design: not every family celebrates Thanksgiving, and these work for everyone.

picks.curator_note: The handprint turkey with a feather for every thankful thought. The pack's signature craft.
A paper horn of plenty for the middle of the friendsgiving table.
The Thanksgiving STEM anchor: real engineering with toothpicks and cranberries.
Ten minutes of shaking and the kids made actual butter, the crowd-pleaser.
Burn off the pre-feast wiggles with the gobble-and-dodge classic.
Teamwork disguised as a race. Baskets fill fast when the whole crew runs.
Zero prep, whole group, A-to-Z gratitude in fifteen minutes.
The quiet close to a loud week. Slips of thanks, read aloud.
Let the kids plan the feast: sign-up sheets, ingredient cards, jobs for everyone.
Gratitude with a job to do, the giving-back anchor of the pack.
The holiday heroes get their cards: custodians, cafeteria crew, bus drivers.
The Vault's gratitude classic. Every thankful thought becomes a leaf.

collections.title: Halloween week
collections.when_to_use: October 31 is coming and the class can feel it. Twelve picks that run as a countdown to Halloween - one a day, or a full party-week plan.

picks.curator_note: The spine of the week: thirteen doors, thirteen mini-activities, one opened daily until the 31st.
Every monster comes out different - the dice-draw craft that starts every Halloween week right.
Zero-prep inference practice in a witch hat - cite your clue or it doesn't count.
The not-too-spooky science anchor: same glow sticks, three temperatures, real data.
Pool-noodle broomsticks, full-speed relay - the wiggles-burner of the pack.
Mini pumpkins vs. bottle pins: the rainy-day insurance policy.
Two-ingredient frozen ghosts - the treat activity that needs no oven.
Outgrown costumes find new kids - the community-minded centerpiece.
Paint them kind, deliver them in pairs - trick-or-treating in reverse.
The Vault's allergy-aware must-do - teal pumpkin, non-food treat box, Halloween for every kid.
Freeze in your spookiest pose when the music stops - the party classic.
A respectful Dia de los Muertos craft about remembrance - learning, not dressing up.

collections.title: Winter Lights
collections.when_to_use: December is coming and the room needs a plan: Christmas crafts that teach, Hanukkah and Kwanzaa activities treated with real respect, New Year countdowns with actual math, and winter-break science that works whether or not it snows.

picks.curator_note: Five-point geometry you can hang. The rare craft that's secretly a math lesson.
A greeting card with a working light bulb. The debugging IS the lesson.
Whose top spins longest? Friction and surface, tested properly.
The story behind the holiday, told round-robin, respectful, real, never a costume.
Bold blocks with meanings attached, meaning first, decoration second.
The Nguzo Saba as a discussion game. The winning principle becomes the week's motto.
Build the countdown, then run it, a paper clock that sweeps a real 60 seconds.
Time the drop to land at zero. Miss it? That's called iteration.
Shakers, a 2027 sign, one glorious hallway lap. The new year deserves an entrance.
No cutting, just looking, six-fold symmetry in real snowflake photos.
Frozen toys, warm hands, salt strategy. The rescue parade at the end is mandatory.
Pinecones and peanut butter, then a week of watching who shows up.

collections.title: The whole calendar
collections.when_to_use: One shelf for the whole school year: twelve holidays, one strong pick each, in calendar order. Plan the year in January or rescue a holiday week the night before. It works both ways.

picks.curator_note: January opens loud. Shakers and one hallway lap to start the year like you mean it.
MLK Day with the real speech at the center: hear his dream, then state yours for your own street.
Lunar New Year lanterns. Make them first, then hang the riddle walk on them later in the week.
February's rule is nobody skipped: every kid makes one card and gets one card.
St. Patrick's Day for the youngest kids. Shapes, counting, and a hunt set at knee height.
Spring eggs dyed with onion skins and beets. The pantry does the chemistry.
July 4th handled with care: the real 13-fold ceremony, practiced respectfully.
October's history slot done right, real Indigenous scientists and artists, researched by the kids.
Halloween that includes every kid: the allergy-aware anchor of the whole month.
Diwali's welcome, made in chalk, dot grid, mirrored pattern, hung by the door.
Thanksgiving's signature craft: a feather for every thankful thought.
December closes with the take-home gift parents actually keep.

collections.title: Little Hands, First Years
collections.when_to_use: Built for the youngest kids in the building: every pick here was designed for three-year-olds first. Short runs, big pieces, one rule per game, and honest about what small hands can actually do. The shelf to grab when the little-kid group lands on you at the last minute.

picks.curator_note: The first balance beam is a line of tape. Slow feet, airplane arms, and nobody falls off a line.
Drop, wait, there it is, cause and effect at exactly the speed a three-year-old runs it.
Moving water one squeeze at a time, with the towel counted as part of the job.
Find the shaker that sounds like yours, sealed tight by an adult, matched by ear or by colored dot.
Stomp round, tiptoe round, crawl round. The tiptoe round is harder than it looks.
Adult-built and staple-checked, both ends open. The window greeters have the best job in the room.
The first icebreaker that works at three: roll, catch, 'Hello, Sam.'
A half-full pitcher and a tray underneath. Spills are expected, and wiping them is part of the work.
Three colors on a ring, a short route, and the rule that living things stay where they live.
Tearing is the skill scissors come after. Glue on the sheet, palm-pat, done when they say so.
The shelf's old faithful, sorting by color with big pieces and no way to be wrong.
Big brushes, big paper, whole-arm strokes, painting at the scale a three-year-old's shoulder actually works at.

collections.title: Little Hands, Next Steps
collections.when_to_use: The second shelf for the youngest kids in the building: twelve more activities designed for three-year-olds first, the first-ever STEM, team, and rainy-day records written for that room, plus the copying games and quiet stations a three-year-old day actually runs on. Grab it when First Years has been through the rotation and the little-kid group is still yours next week.

picks.curator_note: Let go, don't push. A fair test, run at knee height, with a block that refuses to roll and teaches the most.
One leaf, one lens, one full minute of looking. The palm-print practice round is the discovery that hooks them.
Every hand touches every delivery. Seated lines count in full. Ready hands are the only rule.
Walked, never run, with a sit-down ending. The slowest final round gets the biggest laugh in the building.
Feet on islands, floor is the sea. Flat cushions only. A wobbling island is a different game.
One kid, one move, the whole circle copies it back. Copying is the compliment. Name it out loud.
Patterns of one, two, three taps, grown one tap at a time. Needs nothing but knees.
Rough, smooth, soft. A hunt run by hand, where a kid who sees differently is the natural leader.
Peel, carry, pat flat. Loosen the sheets first or you will spend the session peeling for twenty kids.
Big soft rings on a tied-down rope. Threading practice with nothing small enough to worry about.
The river widens one hand-width at a time, and stepping in it is never failing. It is practising.
Adult-built, door always open, three readers at a time. Fort volume is the soft voice a small roof asks for.

collections.title: Little Hands, Third Shelf
collections.when_to_use: The third shelf for the youngest kids in the building: twelve more activities designed for three-year-olds first, the first holiday records ever written for that room, a second and third seasons and rainy-day shelf, and the landing, crossing and trail-following skills a three-year-old day actually runs on. Grab it when Next Steps has been through the rotation and the little-kid group is still yours next week.

picks.curator_note: Five fingers fold down to one, and only then does the ball fall. The long pause at 'two' is where the laughing lives.
Roll, walk down, roll again. The White House has run this since 1878, and the fetching is half the activity.
Walking first, stomping last, and only at the final puddle. Boots learn the difference before the splash is earned.
Nobody touches the cup. The marker lines tell the whole story. That water was the top of the cup.
The ticket block travels hand to hand before the train may leave. Drivers swap every two stops, without a fuss.
A chair boat counts in full. The boat is the rowing and the song, the cardboard was only the costume.
Two stacks, one plank, a toy that walks it. 'Longer bridge, more bend' is real engineering at three.
One ball, kept low, visited person to person. Holding one thing still together is the hard part, and they do it first.
Make your sound and find your match. Found pairs become landmarks the still-searching kids navigate by.
Stand on the arrow, point, say 'that way', then walk. Reading comes before following, every single arrow.
Hands up, song gets big; hands down, it shrinks. End on a whisper the whole room has to lean in for.
Land like a cat and hold for the count of three. Stepping across counts. The skill is stopping on purpose.

collections.title: Little Hands, Fourth Shelf
collections.when_to_use: The fourth shelf for the youngest kids in the building: twelve more activities designed for three-year-olds first, a lantern carried with two hands, eight lights counted as they go on, paper puddles you are supposed to step in, and the carrying, pouring, rocking and delivering jobs a three-year-old day actually runs on. Grab it when the first three shelves have been through the rotation and the little-kid group is still yours next month.

picks.curator_note: Two hands on the handle, walking feet, lantern stays up. The row of lights on the rug at the end was carried there by them.
Place one, switch it on, count from one together. Recounting every time is not slow. It is the practice.
Pointing is the participation. The kid who calls 'still!' has to convince the whole group, then a gust ruins it, correctly.
Walk out, turn around: a line of prints where there was nothing. The snow keeps the record; nothing gets written down.
Step IN every puddle, both feet, every time. Standing in a puddle you are allowed to stand in is the whole game.
One cube at a time, tongs only. The last cubes are the slipperiest, and by then the group knows why, melting.
'The stone went down. The stone is heavier.' That sentence, said together, is a science report at three.
The wagon only goes when both pullers are holding on. Count the cargo in, count it out. They must match.
The toy does the talking, so shy voices get a brave front. A whisper relayed by the adult counts in full.
Find a friend wearing the colour and stand WITH them. Nobody is out, and the finding job is the bigger one.
Half full, two hands, water on the soil. The soil-checker reports 'wet now', a real job, really done.
The humming makes the rocking smaller, and nobody had to be told. End on stillness, held for a count of five.

collections.title: Little Hands, Just Three
collections.when_to_use: The different shelf for the youngest kids in the building: twelve activities banded for three-year-olds ONLY, one shake of one tambourine, a raindrop followed down the glass, lids that fit their pots, a teddy carried to bed without waking him. The four shelves beside this one serve three-to-six; these twelve belong to the threes alone. Grab it for a young-threes room, a first month of program, or any group whose oldest kid just turned three.

picks.curator_note: One piece, one palm-press, one count. The tree fills at exactly the speed a three-year-old decorates, and taking it down counts backwards.
Warm on this hand, cool on that one, a minute apart. The comparison IS the science, and it only works at a stand-still pace.
Umbrella up means get dry. Walked, never run. The weather-worker with the shaker holds the most powerful job in the room.
Your drop merging into a bigger one is not losing it. It is what rain does, reported like news. Needs a real rainy day; refuse to fake it.
'It sticks! It doesn't.' Those two sentences are the data, and the trays are the graph. Encased wands only, the record says why.
Four corners, one passenger, walking feet. The hush-crew's whisper-report at the bed, 'He's asleep', is the teamwork certificate.
Five minutes, no materials, a room that knows itself. A whispered name gets the same echo and the same two claps as a shouted one.
Count the puffs, read the pretend time. Seven o'clock belongs to the blower, and the seeds trying to grow is the true part.
The music is the waiting as much as the shake. One instrument, whole circle, and a tambourine put to sleep properly at the end.
It sticks and it un-sticks, so nothing can be put in the wrong place. Leave it up all day. Moving the picture IS the craft.
The hug is the seatbelt and the flag-caller runs the hill. Check the slope with your own body before any kid rolls it.
A wobble is information, not failure, and finding the trick lid that fits nothing is the result the whole table celebrates.

collections.title: Little Hands, Just Three More
collections.when_to_use: The second shelf banded for three-year-olds ONLY, a bud counted with one fingertip, a heart carried in two hands, a banner that only arrives if every hand walks together, a house painted by its own tenants. The first Just Three shelf proved the band works; these twelve keep narrowing the one honest gap left in the archive, the distance between the threes and everybody else. Reach for it in a young-threes room, a first month of program, or any group whose oldest kid just turned three.

picks.curator_note: One heart, two hands, one named friend, and the adult's list quietly guarantees every kid both gives one and gets one.
One finger, one bud, one number. The touch is how a three-year-old keeps count, and the promised revisit makes it data.
Nothing real goes in and nobody tastes it. Dinosaur soup is legitimate in this kitchen, and five counted circles is a finished stir.
Fingertips for drizzle, palms for the five-second downpour. The silence after the storm is the sound worth sitting in.
The bottle fills from the bottom up and the top fills last, said out loud, over a tray that makes missing safe.
A hand every few steps or it folds. The halfway stop, holding it level together, is harder than the walking. They can feel it.
Every way of arriving gets copied by the whole room, at the teller's size. Wheels are a first-class movement here.
A real minute of held quiet outdoors. The tree will be making those sounds all day; they stopped long enough to hear them.
One line out, the same line back, whole. A small singer echoed by the entire room is a first solo with the room as instrument.
Paint goes on the house, brushes stay at the house. Then the craft dries and becomes the room's new building for days.
Nobody is ever out and nobody is sent back. Said as a promise on the start line, and the whole line lands at the gate together.
A near-match held up to the light is the favourite discovery. Every finished pair gets rolled into a ball, real laundry, done.

collections.title: Little Hands, Just Three, Again
collections.when_to_use: The third shelf banded for three-year-olds ONLY, a welcome written in lamplight along a floor path, every kid in the room holding up the same hard-won three fingers, a snowball that outgrows its rollers, a heart's own beat tapped on knees. Three waves of this kind have narrowed the threes' gap by a third without one record a three-year-old is merely tolerated by. Reach for it in a young-threes room, a first month of program, or any group whose oldest kid just turned three.

picks.curator_note: Two hands carry the lamp; the adult's hand brings the light. The welcome is half built, and the group can SEE it is.
Snow sticks to snow, said once and felt for twenty minutes. The ball outgrowing its crew is a ceremony, not a failure.
First the roads, then the driving. Two cars meeting is traffic, handled the town way: one waits, one passes slowly.
The one drawing medium with no wrong marks in it. The window keeps nothing, and the fading is the frame.
Directors direct, the shadow obeys: nearer the light, bigger the shadow, two facts, both visible, both theirs.
Slow hands keep the water, a rule no adult announced. The sponge taught it, and a team keeps what it discovers.
Every version of three in the room is correct, wobbles copied faithfully. Eighteen different threes is the group portrait.
Counted with eyes, greeted by number, touched by nobody, the path belongs to its residents until the ground dries.
Fast after marching, slower after resting, tapped on knees both times. A drum every musician carries everywhere.
Dip, press, lift straight: the lifting is the printing. A sideways lift makes the mural's first comet, and it stays.
Reaching the wall is the achievement; the patch is a decoration on it. Fetching at a walk is part of the turn.
One hand holds, one hand works, every zip on every coat, discovered at a board where no coat is waiting.

collections.title: Little Hands, Just Three, Once More
collections.when_to_use: The fourth shelf banded for three-year-olds ONLY, a pretend pot of gold collected coin by clinking coin, fireflies counted by their blinks and never caught, a beanbag that falls and gets picked up by its own walker. Four waves of this kind have now cut the threes' gap by nearly half without one record a three-year-old is merely tolerated by. Reach for it in a young-threes room, a first month of program, or any group whose oldest kid just turned three.

picks.curator_note: The pot sounds fuller as the coins land. A job half done you can HEAR. The story stays a story, said out loud.
Catch nothing, jar nothing: the count is kept in chorus through long quiet watches, and the quiet is the activity.
Up one side, a sit at the top, down the other. The summit sit gets its full moment, beheld by the whole line.
The sled departs on the rider's word, 'Ready!', and the pulling adjusts to every rider's review, out loud.
Found by Maya's nose: a name, a description, or an honest 'I don't know'. Every report is a complete turn.
No grid, no outline: where does MY piece belong is the real quilter's job, and crooked squares stay placed.
The song chooses the wearer. Two sentences in a ridiculous hat is exactly how much courage an introduction takes.
Tickly-cool, smooth, soft-moving, warm-squishy, four feelings reported in foot words, wince and giggle included.
Stopping together is the hardest thing a band can do. The silence is practised first, before any lids come out.
Sky first, clouds after. The white arrives as an event. A sleeve is not a brush; the sky takes every style.
It fell, you fixed it, you are walking, from THAT spot, never from the start. Falls are part of walking.
The peg was hungry: more card in the mouth. A row built by the right hands, then unbuilt, the second skill.

collections.title: Little Hands, Just Three, a Fifth Time
collections.when_to_use: The fifth shelf banded for three-year-olds ONLY, a ribbon-wand parade walked for the country's birthday, ants counted as they cross on a road the watchers never touch, one chime note each, struck only when the pointer lands. Five waves of this kind have now cut the threes' gap by more than half without one record a three-year-old is merely tolerated by. Reach for it in a young-threes room, a first month of program, or any group whose oldest kid just turned three.

picks.curator_note: Walking feet, wands in the air: the parade's own fireworks are ribbons, waved fast for ten seconds at the finish line.
A colour counts when two counters agree they can see it. The tree will have changed its answer by next week.
The grown-up makes the rain; the counters count it by ear, eyes closed, ears only, checked against honest fingers.
Clouds drift, they do not bounce: small waves only, and the still-air moment is the crew's to make together.
The basin is the only referee this laboratory recognises. The surprise object fools everybody, kindly.
A pretend picnic, said out loud, no food on the blanket, so every child in the room is equally at the table.
Every feeling is a right answer. The circle copies the drawer's face kindly, at the drawer's own size.
Feet behind the line, hands behind the line: the road belongs to the ants, and it is still going at bedtime.
Your note is still coming. Mallets rest until the pointer lands. Waiting with a promise inside it.
One leaf each, smudges and all: leaves in nature are every shape there is. That leaf grew THAT way. It stays.
Hands stay home; only breath works up there. A puff that moves the feather one inch is a complete rescue.
Flat buttons only: turn it flatter, and the box takes it. The shake at the end is the sound of all of them together.

collections.title: Little Hands, Just Three, a Sixth Time
collections.when_to_use: The sixth shelf banded for three-year-olds ONLY, a smile passed face to face round a whole circle, a puddle holding the sky until one toe closes the picture, one rainstick tipped so slowly its rain takes a minute to fall. Six waves of this kind have now cut the threes' gap from 102 to 30 without one record a three-year-old is merely tolerated by. Reach for it in a young-threes room, a first month of program, or any group whose oldest kid just turned three.

picks.curator_note: Every dream is a right dream, said out loud, echoed whole, and never ranked. That is how dreams start travelling.
Eyes cannot weigh and eyes cannot warm: the palms read the day and report it. 'This hand is holding summer.'
The bus never moves; the travelling is paying, listening for YOUR stop, and getting off like you mean it.
Feet stay planted like tunnel walls. Six feet of tunnel is a journey, and the roof salute is earned.
Eyes cannot weigh. Hands can. The twin bags fool every eye in the room and no hands at all.
Nobody holds anybody up, and the whole thing stands anyway. That is the trick this room now knows.
It left as my smile. It has been on every face in the circle. One smile, nobody left out of its journey.
A picture that only exists while nobody touches it, and the puddle is already mending it.
Seven rains fell in this room today, and not one of them was hurried. Slower... slower still.
Flat palms, gentle press, lift straight: every pillow leaves its circle. Popping is for another day entirely.
Arms in, legs together, roll on: some rolled straight, some rolled wandering, and every log arrived.
Turn the bead until its hole faces the point. The small knock of a bead arriving home, at six different paces.

collections.title: Little Hands, Just Three, a Seventh Time
collections.when_to_use: The seventh shelf banded for three-year-olds ONLY. A name rung on a good bell and answered any way at all, a tissue snowfall watched the whole way down, warm hands lent palm to palm until both pairs agree. Seven waves of this kind have now cut the threes' gap from 102 to 18 without one record a three-year-old is merely tolerated by. Reach for it in a young-threes room, a first month of program, or any group whose oldest kid just turned three.

picks.curator_note: A true story, told plainly, about the first people of this place. Their name said properly by every child in the circle.
We look at the LEAF. We never look at the sun. The glow does the teaching: spring leaves are thin enough for light to get in.
It turned twice. It landed on its corner. It took a LONG time. Slowness, noticed, is the entertainment.
One word, big and plain: FLOAT or SINK, and the sponge, watched long enough, honestly earns both.
Warmth is the thing you can give away and keep. Hands meet by invitation, and waiting is a complete answer.
Ten socks, five truths, no orphans. A wrong sock goes back softly and the finding goes on.
We made weather, and then we STOPPED it. The sky cannot do that. You can.
One ring. One name. One answer, in any form at all, and a name not answered is rung again later, kindly, never louder.
The band marched nowhere and arrived everywhere, and stopped as one band, on one raised hand.
Torn by hand, stuck inside one huge shared sun. A torn edge is the correct edge, every time.
One slow river per dancer, drawn in the air. A dropped ribbon is part of the river, and the river rests when it rests.
Arriving is the whole course: one crossing, at the crosser's own pace, with a hand offered and never required.

collections.title: Little Hands, Just Three, an Eighth Time
collections.when_to_use: The eighth shelf banded for three-year-olds ONLY, a plant given a drink and a promise on Earth Day, a rainbow watched for at a sprinkler's edge, a bear hummed to sleep by a circle with no words at all. Eight waves of this kind have now cut the threes' gap from 102 to 6 without one record a three-year-old is merely tolerated by. Reach for it in a young-threes room, a first month of program, or any group whose oldest kid just turned three.

picks.curator_note: You were thirsty, and somebody came, a drink poured slow, a promise stone set down gently, and the keeping left where the room walks past it daily.
Rainbows are not ours to order. The rain is still ours, one slow walk through a whole summer shower in four steps.
Found five times, once by a nose, nobody hid alone, nobody sought alone, and the finding belonged to everybody.
Built twice, and the second one knew more: a lean is information, a fall is data, and a rocked brick gets a second chance.
Two hands here, two hands there, nine cloths waving because the room hung its own washing, two corners at a time.
Your face knew mine: a copy that wanders is not wrong, it is a new face, and new faces get copied back.
Seven clouds were something today and the group caught them being it, whole arm pointed, before they went back to weather.
The doing was the picture: painted in water, shining while it lasted, handed back by the sun so the fence can hold a hundred more.
Down is where it rests, not where it loses. The flight's count belongs to the whole circle, and every hand owns a share.
In... up it rides. Out... down it comes. A breath nobody had to be taught, carrying a buddy the whole watch.
One hit, one hit back. The listening in between is part of the music, and the silences were music too.
No words at all: a tune hummed small enough to fit under a blanket, and a room that made itself quiet enough to rock in.

collections.title: Just Teens, a First Time
collections.when_to_use: The first shelf banded for thirteen- and fourteen-year-olds ONLY, a tree adopted for a year, a seed library with honest labels, referees running their own tournament, clue chains marked by the strangers who ran them. Reach for it with a teen group that has outgrown the younger shelves and can smell borrowed content at fifty paces: everything here was written for the room it will be used in.

picks.curator_note: Custodians, not owners, a tree measured monthly for a year, and a log that outlives the group that started it.
Eight out of ten sprouted means eight out of ten sprouted: the library's labels are its trays' numbers, and its loans are repaid in seed.
A bearing is a promise your feet keep. Set by one team, run by another, and marked on the honesty of the numbers.
The whistle is a service, not a weapon: teens keep the sheets, run the protocol, and sign their calls.
The floor never notices the join. Six pairs of hands, one continuous session, and the next DJ's opening never spent.
A clue is fair when a stranger could solve it, and the architects watch in silence while the strangers find out.
The seat is warm, never hot: screened questions, an absolute pass, and answers sized by their owners.
Fixed is a verdict the owner gives, triage, benches, charts, and the professional courage of 'beyond this cafe'.
Midnight is a place before it is a time, met city by city, with the arithmetic checked and every greeting practised.
One variable at a time, or the data is weather, not evidence, revolutions and lifted clips overrule every favourite.
A conversation with people who are not in the room, other minds, copied by hand, indexed under your own themes.
Teaching is the final exam nobody grades: a promise made to real children, kept or not kept in their hands.

collections.title: Just Teens, a Second Time
collections.when_to_use: The second shelf banded for thirteen- and fourteen-year-olds ONLY. The floor shelf: a compost heap read by thermometer, a frost forecast graded by its mornings, summer kept in jars, a path maintained under permission, a sky hosted for families, a stream graded by its own citizens, a circuit designed by its coaches, and games invented to survive strangers. Reach for it when the teen room needs work with real responsibility in the band's three thinnest categories, seasons, outdoor, and movement, written for the room itself, not borrowed from younger shelves.

picks.curator_note: The heap is alive, and the ledger is how you know, layers, a turning rota, and a core temperature taken weekly in the same ink, up or down.
A forecast is a promise you check in the morning. A signed call at the board each evening, graded right, wrong, or lucky at dawn.
A jar sealed properly is summer kept, one tested recipe followed exactly, prep by teens, processing by the adult, every batch vouched for in the day book.
Leave the path better than the weather left it, drainage, waymarks and an honest crew book, under a permission whose edges are respected exactly.
Darkness is the venue; the hosts protect it. Red light only, a rehearsed tour of tonight's real sky, and a meteor tally never improved in the retelling.
The stream grades itself; the watch just reads the marks, temperature, clarity, and citizens counted at the same points, then returned unharmed.
A station earns its place by being doable well when tired, proposed, tested on the designers, cut or kept by evidence, then coached.
A rule that only works when everyone is being nice is not a rule yet, strangers break it, the log records it, the card is rewritten.

collections.title: Just Teens, a Third Time
collections.when_to_use: The third shelf banded for thirteen- and fourteen-year-olds ONLY, the floor-raising shelf: seeds given their winter, a field line surveyed square by square, a long rope turned for everyone's courage, a choir holding two lines at once, a radio play recorded in one take per scene, an interview that introduces the person actually met, a whole publication folded from one sheet, and a new year folded in by the tray. Reach for it when the teen room needs the band's eight thinnest categories, seasons, outdoor, movement, music, rainy-day, icebreakers, crafts and holidays, written for the room itself, not borrowed from younger shelves.

picks.curator_note: Cold is an ingredient, and the calendar is the recipe, jars of logged winter, weekly rounds, and a spring test that grades the bank in numbers.
The line does not move; that is what makes it evidence, quadrats at fixed intervals, named only as far as the guide honestly carries.
The rope belongs to the turners; the jumping belongs to everyone. Height, beat and rescue, with the crew's mark chalked honest, landed or not.
Blending is listening louder than you sing, two lines learned apart until boring, then held together, falls and joins in the same log.
The audience believes its ears; the studio's job is to deserve that, actors, a hand-made Foley table, one take and at most one retake per scene.
You introduce the person you actually met, not the one you expected. Three questions, a partner's own words on the card, and the right to strike any line.
Eight pages, one sheet, no editor but the maker, planned on the map, lettered in the flat order, and traded only after being read entire.
Every fold is a signature the steamer will read, teens fold and tally by the tray, the adult alone runs the steamer, and the feast is eaten together.

collections.title: Just Teens, a Fourth Time
collections.when_to_use: The fourth shelf banded for thirteen- and fourteen-year-olds ONLY, the floor-to-eight shelf: garlic planted in autumn for a summer harvest, bats counted out of a roost at dusk, a no-contact game won by the catch, a song taken apart and rearranged, a documentary filmed with consent before camera, introductions answered with feet first, a blank book bound by hand, and sunlight trialled one variable at a time. Reach for it when the teen room needs the band's eight thinnest categories, seasons, outdoor, movement, music, rainy-day, icebreakers, crafts and STEM, written for the room itself, not borrowed from younger shelves.

picks.curator_note: You plant for a harvest you will hand to summer, cloves pointed up at a measured depth, the winter logged honestly, spring emergence counted shoot by shoot.
Count what leaves; never chase what returns, sectors, silence and tallies by the minute from one set watch point, and no bat ever approached.
The catch is the defence, shots rebound off a frame, the forbidden zone stays empty, and landings are judged once, settled and chalked.
An arrangement is an argument about what the song is. One change at a time, predictions written before they are heard, verdicts in the same ink.
Consent comes before camera, every time, a true film about one real room, its subjects seeing the cut before any other audience.
Your feet answer first; then you get to explain, a room sorts itself along a line, then talks across the whole distance of its disagreement.
A book is a machine you can make by hand, grain with the spine, holes measured before they are punched, a stitch inspected by a friend.
Sunlight is slow; the log is how you know it is working, a shared control, one variable at a time, and a void trial declared without flinching.

collections.title: Just Teens, a Fifth Time
collections.when_to_use: The fifth shelf banded for thirteen- and fourteen-year-olds ONLY. The floor-to-nine shelf: a season's heat counted in degree-days and a budburst predicted in ink, one yard mapped into its many microclimates, a three-team game with one enormous ball, a room conducted by learned hands, a museum of loaned objects on one table, counted sashiko stitches in indigo and white, introductions toured across drawn countries, and a true Celtic knot traced strand by strand. Reach for it when the teen room needs the band's eight thinnest categories, seasons, outdoor, movement, music, rainy-day, crafts, icebreakers and holidays, written for the room itself, not borrowed from younger shelves.

picks.curator_note: A plant keeps its calendar in heat, not in dates, daily degree-days in one ledger, a prediction in ink, and the plant itself does the grading.
One yard holds many climates. Twelve stations read inside one ten-minute window, drawn as a map that anyone can check with a thermometer.
Three teams, one ball, no owner. Serve by calling a colour, lift everything, and win by being the team the ball cannot catch out.
Your hands speak first; the room answers, patterns in two, three and four, cues that land, and a cut-off whose silence counts as music.
A museum is an argument made of objects, loans under law, labels checked by their owners, and every object signed home entire.
Small stitches, counted rows, no loose ends, a centuries-old stitch learned on scrap first, its wandering rows unpicked by their own makers.
Draw the country only you know, three-station tours of the places that made you, and blank regions that stay blank, unasked, entire.
One line, no beginning it will admit to, over, under, over, traced all the way home before a drop of ink is allowed near it.
